title: Emerson close
hookLine: the last day with the sage of Concord: go back out under the stars
carry: look as if for the first time

cards: Go back to where this all started. A young minister has left his pulpit in conscience. His wife Ellen has died.
And in his first book, Nature, he asks the reader for something simple: go out alone at night and look up at the stars.

Since then this path has followed him a long way: the snowstorm behind the preacher, trust thyself, another circle around every circle, a friend who asked who gets to think, a town that rebuilt his roof, an old man who forgot names and kept his kindness.
Today is the last day with the sage of Concord, and the best way to close isn't a summary. It's to go back outside.

teach.h: STARS ONCE IN A THOUSAND YEARS.
teach.b: First, the stars. Early in Nature, Emerson imagines the stars appearing only one night in a thousand years. People, he says, would believe and adore, and remember that night for generations.
Instead they come out every night, and we barely look. His complaint isn't that the world is dull. It's that we've gotten used to it.
On a bare common at twilight, he writes, something lifts in him: "I become a transparent eye-ball; I am nothing; I see all." It's a strange image, and some readers have teased him for it.

But the point is clear enough: for a moment the little self, with its worries, steps aside, and there is only seeing. Third, how the long walk circles back. Self-reliance meant trusting your own eyes.
Days meant noticing what each ordinary day holds out. Even his limits came down to sight: what his bright gaze missed.

teach.h: SO MUCH COMES BACK TO LOOKING.
teach.b: So much of Emerson comes back to looking. Fourth, what to take out the door. Not a theory.
Look at something familiar as if you had never seen it: a sky, a hand, a face across the table.
Some traditions call this wonder, some call it attention, some call it seeing God in all things, and some just call it waking up. Emerson didn't need a name for it.

teach.h: LOOK AS IF FOR THE FIRST TIME.
teach.b: He wanted people to stand where they already were, and look as if for the first time.

how: Readers who finish a season with Emerson often return to the opening of Nature, and to the simple habit it describes: going outside and looking at the sky as if seeing it for the first time.

games.q: Emerson asks you to imagine it: the stars appear only one night in a thousand years. what does he say people would do?
o: barely notice, like any other night.
believe and adore, and remember it for generations.
measure them and write it down.
games.why: he says they would believe and adore, and remember the night for generations. his point: the stars come out every night, and we barely look.

practice: If you can, step out a door or stand by a window and let your eyes rise to the sky, whatever it's doing: blue, gray, stars, a ceiling of streetlight.
Pretend this sky appears only once in a thousand years, and you happen to be here for it. Don't name things or take a photo; when your mind wanders back to your list, just look up again.

wordCard.voice: Emerson close. The end of this path's long walk with the sage of Concord, ending where his first book began: outside, alone, looking up. Today's word.
